item.title: Girard fermat conjecture
item.description:
Source: TW

There is a remarkable theorem of Albert Girard that states that any prime number of the form p = 4*k+1 (where k is some integer) is the sum of two integer squares: p=a^2+b^2. Fermat later stated the same theorem to Mersenne on Christmas of 1640; hence, some people call it the Christmas theorem. However, neither of them provided a proof, which was later provided by Leonhard Euler. 5 =1^2+2^2 13 = 3^2+4^2 17 = 1^2+4^2 29 = 2^2+5^2 Mathematicians say that this simple-looking result has profound ramifications. Given that p= a^2 + b^2; if we plot (a, b), we get a 45-degree sector between 45 and 90 degrees. Overall, the distribution of points in this sector is uniform as p goes to $\infty$. The primes of the form p=1^2+b^2 as b increases will have an angle closer to 90 degrees. Primes of the form p=a^2+b^2 where $a \approx b$ will have an angle of 45 degrees.
